newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Malaysia, Indonesia close to buying Indian meal.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia, Indonesia close to buying Indian meal.

text.p: Indonesia and Malaysia are close to buying about 10,000-20,000 tonnes each of Indian-origin soymeal for nearby shipment but the rest of the market may soon lapse into a holiday swoon, regional traders said on Thrusday.

"Indonesia and Malaysia are looking at Indian-meal at a price of around US$290 a tonne C&F while the sellers are at $295. It could be done today," the general manager of a European commodity house told Reuters.
Indian-origin meal coming into Southeast Asia was being quoted by regional traders at around $295-$300 a tonne C&F for January/February shipment on a Tweendecker.

"The Malaysians were talking of a price of about $290 (a tonne C&F) and below. They want something like 20,000 tonnes of meal. The Indonesians may be in for about 10,000-15,000 tonnes of meal," a dealer for another European commodity company said.
A dealer for a U.S. trading house said that if both sides reach an agreement on the price, "Indonesia and Malaysia will probably get a few cargoes of meal altogether."
A senior dealer said the two countries need to buy some soymeal "because there's a bit of a shortage developing in meal down there."
Thailand stayed out of the market, dealers said.
"The Thais were thinking the market will come down, but the market moved up last night. They will probably sit it out for now until prices come down to a level they like," one said.
In another development, Malaysian buyers who earlier were looking at picking up at least one Panamax-sized vessel of corn decided to back away from the market after prices in the U.S. held steady.

"The Malaysians were looking at a price for corn of about $140-$143 a tonne C&F. But, if anything, the prices this week even inched up compared to the level last week," a U.S. commodity house dealer said.
"The Malaysians were definitely in the market for some corn, but they decided against buying because of price considerations," a trader said.
The price of U.S. corn coming into the region was seen at around $147-$149 a tonne C&F for February/April shipment on board a Panamax against last week's quote of $146-$148 a tonne C&F, dealers said.
Prices of the December corn contract on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) rose $1 on Wednesday to end at $2.67-1/2 a bushel. Corn was bouncing between $2.65-$2.68 a bushel last week.
The rest of the grains and oilseeds market remains slow with the Christmas and New Year holidays expected to further dampen business over the coming week, dealers said.

"It's the silly season," a dealer for U.S.-based trading house said. "You'll see dribs and dabs of business being done, but a lot of people are going to walk away from the market and take a look again after the New Year."
Another trader said most of the players in the market seem ready to take a break for the holidays.
"All over Southeast Asia, it's been relatively quiet. Maybe something will be done after the holidays," the dealer said.
One trader said there was virtually no excitement in the market over the release of the December crop report of the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) on Friday.
"People are waiting more for the January crop report. The demand side of the business here is cooling off," he said.
